item.title: Leadership and Governance in Complex Learning Systems: Risk, Knowledge and Entrepreneurship
item.content:encoded:
Enis Elezi, University of Westminster

Knowledge-intensive organisations face mounting complexity from resource constraints, digitalisation, accountability demands, and geopolitical pressures. Existing research on these challenges remains fragmented across disciplinary silos and often lacks systemic understanding of how these institutions observe, interpret and respond to complexity.

This special issue integrates typically isolated scholarly conversations about leadership, governance, risk, knowledge and entrepreneurship within a cybernetic framework. It explores the interconnected processes of observation, communication, decision and learning that enable organisations to adapt and remain viable across sectors including universities, health systems, research institutes and public agencies.

Appel publié par Kybernetes. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Leadership and governance as systemic architectures of observation, decision and learning
  • Enterprise-wide risk management, knowledge management and entrepreneurship as interconnected cybernetic processes
  • Cross-sector analyses of universities, health systems, research institutes, public agencies and professional service firms as complex learning systems
  • Reflexive and second-order perspectives on how organisations construct and revise their own governance arrangements
  • Theory-as-method applications using cybernetics, systems thinking or complexity frameworks

Timeline

  • January 26, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • December 26, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Management in Emerging, Developing, and Transition Economies: Context, Mechanisms, and Outcomes
item.content:encoded:
Most management research has been developed in Western contexts, leaving significant gaps in understanding leadership and organizational practices in emerging, developing, and transition economies—regions that now generate nearly half of global economic output. These economies operate under distinct institutional conditions where formal institutions are incomplete or unevenly enforced, requiring firms to rely on alternative coordination mechanisms and making context a primary determinant of business strategy and performance.

This special issue addresses this literature gap by centering emerging, developing, and transition economies as objects of theoretical inquiry rather than control variables. It invites studies across governance, entrepreneurship, sustainability, and leadership that examine how management practices evolve, adapt, or are translated when formal rules and infrastructures cannot be taken for granted. The call welcomes quantitative surveys, experiments, qualitative ethnographies, mixed-methods research, and conceptual work, particularly comparative studies spanning regions or contrasting different institutional settings.

Appel publié par Baltic Journal of Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How and with what consequences do firms substitute private or community governance for missing or unreliable formal institutions, and which mechanisms make these substitutes durable or fragile?
  • Which configurations of resources, networks, and legitimacy enable opportunity discovery and scaling in thin or nascent markets, and how do founders and top managers navigate uncertainty and institutional gaps across growth stages?
  • Under resource constraints and uneven enforcement, what capability bundles allow firms to align environmental initiatives with competitive outcomes, and how do local cultural or state priorities shape these trajectories?
  • How do reporting, budgeting, and control systems adapt when enforcement is uneven, and what are the implications for investment, innovation, market signals, and stakeholder trust in emerging markets?
  • How do contextual communication and power structures condition the effectiveness of leadership, employee voice, engagement, and performance systems in transition settings, and what are the boundary conditions for transferability?
  • How do commitments to learning and open innovation translate into performance when institutions are in flux, and which organisational routines, such as bricolage, mediate these effects?
  • How do political ties, state ownership, or party networks shape strategic decision-making, board dynamics, and accountability in firms and hybrid organisations operating under volatile or contested regulatory regimes?
  • How do gender, ethnicity, and other social cleavages intersect with institutional voids to shape leadership careers, informal influence, and patterns of inclusion and exclusion inside organisations?
  • In conflict-affected, fragile, or post-disaster settings, which leadership practices and governance arrangements enable organisational resilience, continuity of services, and recovery, and what trade-offs do they imply?
  • How do regional, cross-border, or diaspora networks among managers, professionals, and researchers mediate the transfer, translation, and contestation of management ideas and leadership models across institutional contexts?

Timeline

  • January 12, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • January 4, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Leadership and Change in M&As
item.content:encoded:
David Kroon, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Olimpia Meglio, University of Naples "Federico II"

Nicola Mirc, Toulouse School of Management

Audrey Rouzies, Toulouse School of Management

Satu Teerikangas, Turku University

Mergers and acquisitions serve as significant catalysts for organizational change, enabling leaders to reshape organizational boundaries and develop new capabilities. However, their implications extend far beyond the merging firms to affect employees, managers, customers, and communities. While M&A research has explored various themes and theoretical perspectives, most special issues have adopted narrow lenses focusing on single aspects like organizational culture or post-merger integration, leaving fundamental questions about how these large-scale transformations unfold.

M&As represent profound episodes of organizational change that disrupt established structures and challenge existing cultures. Yet research on M&As and change management has largely evolved separately, addressing similar questions about how people respond to uncertainty and how leaders enable adaptation without meaningful cross-fertilization. This special issue seeks to bridge these research communities, offering fresh perspectives on how actors at multiple levels shape M&A outcomes and navigate the tension between strategic ambition and human adaptability.

Appel publié par Journal of Change Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • M&As as continuous change: how firms handle deliberate design versus evolving circumstances, intended versus unintended change trajectories, and seizing opportunities while mitigating threats
  • Leadership and employee change agency in M&As: employees as sense makers, boundary spanners, and informal leaders; proactive versus passive roles in integration
  • Emotions and irrationality in M&As: hubris, anxiety, grief, excitement, overconfidence, and escalation of commitment in M&A decisions and integration
  • Changing relationships in M&As: renegotiating internal relationships among employees, teams, and leaders; external relationships with suppliers, customers, regulators, and communities; trust, social capital, and power dynamics
  • Digitalization and Technology in M&As: AI-driven analytics, ERP systems, collaboration software; digital capabilities as deal drivers; technology's impact on cultural dynamics and integration speed
  • M&As and Grand Challenges: role of M&As in addressing environmental degradation and global crises; economic and social sustainability; M&As as a force for good

Timeline

  • August 1, 2026: Submission starting date
  • October 31, 2026: Closing date

item.title: Grounded in Causality: Elevating Evidence for Leadership Practice
item.content:encoded:
This special issue of The Leadership Quarterly seeks empirical research that advances our understanding of leadership through rigorous causal inference methods. We invite submissions that employ experimental designs, quasi-experimental approaches, longitudinal studies, or other methodologically sound approaches to establish causal relationships in leadership phenomena.

item.title: Leader Behaviours and their Perception across Organizational Levels
item.content:encoded:
Iris K. Gauglitz, University of Bamberg

Peter Harms, University of Alabama's Culverhouse College of Business

Urszula Lagowska, NEOMA Business School

Birgit Schyns, NEOMA Business School

Kimberley Breevaart, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Leadership research increasingly recognizes the importance of examining both leader behaviours and their interpretations across organizational levels. Rather than treating behaviour and perception as competing perspectives, this special issue seeks to integrate them and explore how different organizational actors understand and react to leader actions in complex, modern workplaces.

The issue addresses gaps in current understanding, including how leader behaviours and their perceptions vary outside the leader-follower dyad, discrepancies between leader intentions and follower interpretations, and the effectiveness of leadership development programs. Contributors are encouraged to employ multilevel analytical approaches and diverse methodologies to capture the complexity of leadership dynamics.

Research submissions are invited across multiple areas: theoretical development of multilevel leadership models, investigation of underlying processes and contextual factors affecting behaviour perception, examination of interactions between organizational actors, and methodological innovations in measuring leader behaviour and perceptual biases.

Appel publié par European Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical models proposing new or conceptually advanced configurations of leader behaviour and its perceptions, which consider the role of new working contexts in shaping leader behaviours and their perceptions
  • Multi-level conceptualizations of the impact of leader behaviour at multiple levels of organizations with a view to understand how and why perceptions across levels differ
  • Studies including models that explain why and under which conditions leader behaviour and its perceptions affect workplace outcomes, notably when leaders and others differ in their perceptions/(perceived) intentions or when behaviour is perceived as inconsistent or ambivalent
  • Research that investigates polarisation in follower perceptions—why perceptions of the same behaviour may diverge significantly
  • Studies looking at leader and follower behaviour and their interaction, such as how behaviours from one party trigger behavioural reactions of the other party and what that means for an effective collaboration
  • Studies considering the role of organisational hierarchy in how leaders behave and how their behaviour is perceived
  • Contributions considering interactions between personality traits (e.g., leader–follower trait congruence) in shaping behavioural expressions and perceptual accuracy; team outcomes of leader behaviour, for example, perception differences between team members and how this affects outcomes; and relative leader behaviour, that is, perceptions of how one follower is treated compared to others
  • Studies that develop and validate new measures of leader behaviour (e.g., behavioural indicators)
  • Studies that develop new measures that allow for the measurement of perceptual biases in leadership ratings and studies using advanced statistical approaches (e.g., polynomial regression analyses, multilevel modelling, pattern approaches)

Timeline

item.title: The Interplay of Human Resource Management and Leadership: Alignment, Tensions, and Consequences
item.content:encoded:
Aneeqa Suhail, Tilburg University

Steven Kilroy, Trinity College Dublin

Robin Bauwens, Tilburg University

Sut I Wong, BI Norwegian Business School

Sasa Batistič, Tilburg University

This special issue examines the dynamic relationship between human resource management systems and leadership behaviors, addressing how they align, conflict, or substitute for one another in shaping organizational outcomes. The issue recognizes that while HRM and leadership research have traditionally developed as separate streams, they operate interdependently in practice. Understanding their interplay is essential for comprehending how people management actually functions in organizations and for developing more effective, coherent approaches to managing employees.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How HRM systems and leadership behaviors interact in shaping employee and organizational outcomes across organizational levels
  • Different forms of alignment between HRM and leadership (supplementary fit, complementary fit, perceptual filtering) and their distinct consequences
  • When and how HRM systems function as substitutes for leadership and resulting consequences
  • How misalignment between HRM systems and leadership behaviors emerges, persists, or becomes institutionalized
  • When alignment amplifies negative outcomes such as work intensification, role overload, or employee strain
  • How employees interpret and respond to misalignment or substitution between HRM systems and leadership
  • Which configurations of HRM systems and leadership strengthen effectiveness of remote and hybrid work arrangements
  • How leaders enact, adapt, or resist HRM systems when leading employees at a distance
  • Employee experiences of alignment and misalignment in remote and hybrid work settings
  • How HRM-leadership configurations evolve over time and affect employee and organizational outcomes
  • How temporal shifts in leadership behaviors or HRM systems alter the balance between substitution and complementarity

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Beyond the Code: Understanding How, When and Why Humans Employ Generative AI in Innovation
item.content:encoded:
William Y. Degbey, University of Vaasa

Maria Pajuoja, University of Vaasa

Matti Pihlajamaa, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland

Baniyelme D. Zoogah, McMaster University

Waymond Rodgers, University of Texas

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is defined as the frontier of computational advancements that references human intelligence in addressing ever more complex decision-making problems. A key development is Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, which can process and generate human-like language, extract insights, and produce creative outputs. Gen AI has enormous potential to significantly boost national economies. Its widespread adoption could increase GDP in the EU region by +8% (EUR 1.2–1.4 trillion) over the next ten years, provided innovators are equipped with the necessary skills and capabilities.

Yet, adoption remains uneven. For instance, European countries average a 54 percent adoption rate, below the global average of 61 percent. This uneven adoption is compounded by the global competition for skilled talent and persistent workforce shortages, particularly in digital and AI-related fields. McKinsey estimates that up to 12 million job transitions may be required due to AI, underscoring the urgent need for reskilling and entrepreneurial innovation.

Appel publié par Journal of Managerial Psychology. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How is Gen AI being used in innovation processes at different levels?
  • How do organizations apply Gen AI to replace, reinforce, or reveal innovation activities, and what are the resulting effects on, for example, process efficiency, novelty, and responsiveness to market needs?
  • How do varied patterns of Gen AI use across process phases and organizational levels influence the dynamics and management of innovation processes?
  • How do individual innovators use Gen AI in their work, what influences this usage, and what are the measurable outcomes of AI-augmented innovation efforts in terms of product, service, or process quality and speed?
  • In what ways does Gen AI influence innovation team dynamics, including collaboration, resilience, and decision-making, particularly in virtual or hybrid team environments?
  • What psychological and behavioral effects emerge from using Gen AI in innovation settings, such as changes in employee engagement, collaboration dynamics, or perceptions of autonomy?
  • How do managerial competencies influence the successful implementation of Gen AI in organizational innovation efforts?
  • What organizational capabilities need to be developed to successfully implement, integrate, and support the use of Gen AI in innovation efforts?
  • How are organizations supporting continuous learning and skill development for employees working with Gen AI, and what mechanisms are most effective in enabling the strategic use of Gen AI?
  • What ethical challenges do organizations face when deploying Gen AI in innovation activities, and how are they addressing issues such as intellectual property, transparency, and sociocultural responsibility?

Timeline

  • January 15, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • August 31, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Personality in the Upper Echelons – Advancing Theory, Methods, and Context
item.content:encoded:
Upper echelons research has long argued that organizational outcomes reflect the characteristics of those who lead them. Scholars have shown that personality plays a central role in shaping how executives interpret information, make decisions, interact with stakeholders, and steer their organizations. Yet, despite a rapidly expanding literature on CEO personality and related constructs, recent reviews highlight persistent challenges: conceptual narrowness, methodological limitations, geographic concentration, and a tendency toward insularity rather than theoretical integration.

Appel publié par Journal of Managerial Psychology. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do motives, values, traits, and narratives of organizational leaders shape firm behavior?
  • Under what conditions do personality effects strengthen or weaken?
  • How can scholars better measure personality in the upper echelons?
  • How do institutional, cultural, and governance contexts shape the expression and consequences of executive personality?
  • Broadening the conceptualization of executive personality beyond Big Five and narcissism traits
  • Integrating insights from personality psychology including motives, values, identity, and life stories
  • Mechanisms linking personality to strategic outcomes such as CSR, M&A, innovation, and risk-taking
  • Personality dynamics over time including personality change and developmental experiences
  • TMT dynamics, leadership styles, and power distributions shaped by executive personality
  • Contextual, cultural, and institutional moderators of personality effects across national cultures and governance systems
  • Measurement and assessment of executive personality using multi-method designs and unobtrusive indicators
  • Personality composition and complementarities within boards, TMTs, and collective leadership
  • CEO selection, evaluation, and succession planning incorporating personality
  • Executive personality influence on ethical decision making and societal outcomes

Timeline

  • August 1, 2026: Submission window opens
  • September 30, 2026: Submission window closes
  • December 31, 2026: Decision notification
  • June 1, 2027: Target publication
